questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the passive defense mechanisms in humans. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Passive (or non-specific, first-line) defences are the **barriers that are always present** and that **prevent pathogens from entering the body**, or kill them at the entrance, whether or not an infection has occurred.

**1. Physical barriers**
- **Skin**: a tough, dry outer layer of **keratinised dead cells**, continuously shed, which pathogens cannot easily penetrate.
- **Mucous membranes** of the nose, trachea and gut: the **sticky mucus traps** dust, bacteria and viruses; the **cilia** of the trachea and bronchi **sweep the mucus upwards** to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out.
- **Hairs in the nostrils** and **eyelashes**, and the **flushing action** of tears, saliva and urine.
- **Blood clotting** and **scab** formation seal wounds.

**2. Chemical barriers**
- **Sebum** (oily secretion of the skin) and **sweat** give an acid skin surface (pH 3 to 5) which discourages bacterial growth.
- **Lysozyme** in tears, saliva, sweat and nasal mucus **digests the cell walls of bacteria**.
- **Hydrochloric acid of the stomach** (pH 1.5 to 2) **kills most microbes** swallowed with food.
- **Acid secretions of the vagina** and the flushing action of **urine** keep the urinary and genital tracts clean.

**3. Biological barrier**
- The **normal harmless microbes (flora)** on the skin and in the gut and vagina **compete** with pathogens for food and space and produce substances that inhibit them.

**4. Reflex actions**: **coughing, sneezing, vomiting and diarrhoea** expel pathogens and irritants.

(Any six points well described earn the 6 marks.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What is immunity?

(ii) Outline and explain the different types of immunity in humans. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Immunity** is the **ability of the body to resist or overcome infection by pathogens** (and the effect of their toxins), by recognising **foreign antigens** and destroying them, mainly through **white blood cells (lymphocytes) and antibodies**.

**(ii) Types of immunity**

**1. Innate (natural, inborn) immunity.** Present from birth, **non-specific** and the same against all pathogens: the barriers of question (a), **phagocytes** (neutrophils and macrophages), inflammation and fever, and interferons.

**2. Acquired (adaptive) immunity.** Developed during life, **specific** to one antigen, and with **memory**. It is of two kinds.

| | **Active immunity** | **Passive immunity** |
|---|---|---|
| Who makes the antibodies | The **person's own** lymphocytes (B cells, plasma cells) | **Ready-made antibodies** received from outside |
| Natural | After **catching the disease** (infection) | **Antibodies of the mother** pass to the baby through the **placenta** and in **colostrum and breast milk** |
| Artificial | By **vaccination**: injecting dead or weakened (attenuated) pathogens, or toxoids, which carry antigens but cause no disease | **Injection of serum (antiserum)** containing antibodies, for example **anti-tetanus serum** or **anti-venom** |
| Onset | **Slow** (days to weeks, because lymphocytes must be selected and multiply) | **Immediate** |
| Duration | **Long lasting** (memory cells remain) | **Short lived** (antibodies are broken down, no memory cells) |

**Explanation.** In active immunity the antigen **stimulates the specific B and T lymphocytes to divide**; **plasma cells** secrete antibodies, and **memory cells** remain, so a later infection gives a **faster and stronger secondary response**. In passive immunity the body does not meet the antigen, so **no memory cells** are formed and the protection fades, but it acts at once and is used for emergencies and for newborn babies.

(Marking: 2 marks for the definition, 4 marks for the types with explanation.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Using the ABO blood group system in humans, determine which of the blood transfusions are safe or unsafe and why? *[8 marks]* *(6, 6, 8 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The principle.** The ABO groups depend on **antigens on the surface of the red blood cells** and **antibodies in the plasma**. The plasma never carries the antibody against the person's own antigen.

| Blood group | Antigens on red cells | Antibodies in plasma |
|---|---|---|
| A | A | anti-B |
| B | B | anti-A |
| AB | A and B | none |
| O | none | anti-A and anti-B |

A transfusion is **safe** when **the antigens on the donor's red cells are not recognised by the antibodies in the recipient's plasma**. If they are, the antibodies bind the donor cells and cause **agglutination (clumping)**.

**Donor to recipient**

| Donor / Recipient | A | B | AB | O |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | safe | unsafe | safe | unsafe |
| **B** | unsafe | safe | safe | unsafe |
| **AB** | unsafe | unsafe | safe | unsafe |
| **O** | safe | safe | safe | safe |

**Safe transfusions:** A to A and to AB; B to B and to AB; AB to AB only; O to O, A, B and AB.

**Unsafe transfusions:** A to B and to O; B to A and to O; AB to A, B and to O.

**Why the unsafe ones are dangerous.** For example, group A blood given to a group B person: the recipient's **anti-A antibodies** attach to the **A antigens** of the donor cells, which **agglutinate**. The clumps **block small blood vessels** (capillaries of the kidneys, lungs and brain), the red cells are **haemolysed** (haemoglobin is released), which can cause **kidney failure, shock and death**.

**Special cases.** **Group O** is the **universal donor** (no A or B antigens, and the donor's antibodies are **diluted** in the recipient's large plasma volume); **group AB** is the **universal recipient** (no antibodies in the plasma). The **rhesus (Rh) factor** must also be matched: a rhesus negative person must not receive rhesus positive blood.

(Marking: antigens and antibodies, the safe and unsafe combinations, and the explanation by agglutination.)
